title: How to Track Every Form in GTM With One Listener, Across Nine Platforms
intro:
The agency I work with usually builds a landing page for a client's Google or Facebook ads, unless the client insists on using their own website. That sounds simple until you open the container. The main site might run GoHighLevel, Gravity Forms or Unbounce, while the landing page sits on SwipePages.

So one account had two form platforms, and that meant two listeners to install, update and check, across a lot of accounts. I got tired of it and put them into one script.

This is how that script works and how I set it up, told in the order you'd do it, with a real anonymised container as the example. That container has a Squarespace main site, a SwipePages landing page and one tag covering both. Along the way is the mistake that passes every test and still leaves Enhanced Conversions with nothing to send.
tldr: Import the free container, or paste one Custom HTML tag, and it detects which form platform is on the page. One regex trigger catches every real confirmation across nine platforms. Send that to GA4, split Google Ads by hostname if you run a landing page, map the contact fields to User-Provided Data, then test that ec_email is actually filled in, as well as that the event fired.
sections: What's already out there

Before you take my word for any of this, here are the other options I found when I checked again, because some are a better fit depending on your setup.

OptionWhat it isThe gap for my setup
Choice Universal Form TrackerFree WordPress plugin that sends one event across Contact Form 7, Gravity Forms, Ninja Forms, Elementor Pro and AvadaActively maintained and worth a look if everything is on WordPress. It can't reach a SwipePages landing page
AVAK Form Tracking ListenerWordPress plugin covering five form tools, with errors and abandonmentAlso WordPress only
ListenLayerHosted data layer platform, added with one script through GTMIts form page lists seven tools, without SwipePages or GoHighLevel, and your tracking then depends on their platform
Generic submit listenersA short script on the form's submit eventIts author says iframe embeds may not work, and it doesn't cover consent or duplicates

If your whole client base is on WordPress, a plugin may be all you need. My problem was the mix: hosted landing page builders next to whatever the main site uses, in a GTM container I control. I couldn't find a free tag that covered that mix, though a search like mine can always miss one.
Why a click or a thank-you page isn't a lead

Before writing any of it, I had to decide what should count as a lead. Most containers use one of two signals, and both are wrong in predictable ways. A button click also counts failed validation and rage clicks. A thank-you page also counts refreshes and direct visits, and some forms don't redirect at all.

The better signal is the confirmation the form itself shows after a real submit, an idea I first picked up from Chloe Christine. The hard part is that every platform shows it differently, so the script looks for each platform's own signal:

PlatformSuccess signalEvent prefix
SwipePagesamp-form-submit-success classswipe_form
Gravity Formsgform_confirmation_loaded, confirmation wrapper, postback pagesgf_form
UnbounceConfirmation render after submitunbounce_form
Elementor Prosubmit_success and .elementor-message-successelementor_form
GoHighLevelRender after submit (inline), postMessage (iframe)ghl_form
KartraConfirmation renderkartra_form
WPFormswpformsAjaxSubmitSuccess, confirmation container, postback pageswpforms_form
Squarespace2xx from /api/form/ and the submission messagesquarespace_form
Contact Form 7wpcf7mailsent and data-status="sent"cf7_form

Each platform pushes {prefix}_success and {prefix}_failed, plus ec_form_interaction on first input and ec_tracker_initialized when the script loads. Every event also carries ec_detection_method, so you can see how each lead was detected and segment by it.
Before you start

That's the thinking. To follow along, you'll need:

  • GTM on every page with a form, including landing pages and thank-you pages.
  • Publish access to the container.
  • Your GA4 Measurement ID, and your Google Ads conversion ID and labels if you run ads.
  • A list of any older form tags and thank-you triggers, so you don't count leads twice.
Step 1: Import the container

You don't have to rebuild what took me a while to get right. Once this was working, I packaged it into one file: the listener, GA4 config, page_view, generate_lead, the trigger and the variables. Download the GTM import file, or get it from GitHub.

  1. In GTM, go to Admin > Import Container and choose the file.
  2. Choose a new workspace, then Merge and Rename conflicting tags, triggers and variables.
  3. Read the preview before you confirm. It should show nothing modified or deleted.
  4. Open Const - GA4 Measurement ID and enter your ID.
[[img:uft-import-preview|Merge and Rename selected, with the preview listing what will be added. This container already had some of the same names, so yours may differ.]]
Don't leave it on Overwrite. GTM can default to it, and it replaces your workspace. Also, if your container already has a GA4 config and a page view tag, delete the imported copies or you'll count page views twice.
Downloaded this file before 5 November 2026? Get it again. My first upload still had a test consent tag and a phone variable reading the wrong key. The next steps explain why that matters.

Rather not import? The next step is the same thing by hand.
Step 2: Or add the listener by hand

1. Go to Tags > New > Custom HTML.
  2. Paste the GTM tag file. It includes the <script> wrapper and fits under GTM's 102,400-character limit.
  3. Fire it on All Pages, or Initialization - All Pages as on the store below, or Consent Initialization if your consent tool needs it early.
[[img:uft-listener-tag|The live tag on my example account, which still runs v3.1.0. The config sits at the top.]]
window.EC_FORM_CONFIG = {
  debug: false,            // true only while testing
  hashPii: false,          // true adds ec_email_sha256 and ec_phone_sha256
  rawFields: false,        // keeps ec_raw_fields out of the payload
  defaultCountryCode: '1', // fallback; a country field on the form wins
  countryCodeField: '',    // exact field name holding a country or dial code
  strictSuccess: false     // true drops inferred successes
};

Leave strictSuccess off at first, then decide once you've seen your own ec_detection_method values. Inferred successes like pagehide catch redirects, but they can fire if someone clicks submit and then leaves.

Install one copy per platform. Don't run this tag alongside a single-platform listener for the same form tool, or each lead counts twice.
Step 3: Catch every platform with one trigger

This is where one script pays off. With a listener per platform you'd need a trigger per platform too. Here one regex does it. Go to Triggers > New > Custom Event, tick Use regex matching and use:

^(swipe|gf|unbounce|elementor|ghl|kartra|wpforms|squarespace|cf7)_form_success$
[[img:uft-trigger-regex|The same idea on my example account. The v3.1.0 pattern doesn't have cf7 yet, so copy the one above.]]

Failed submissions get their own trigger if you want them: the same pattern ending in _form_failed$. They carry ec_failed_fields, so you can see which field is stopping people.
Step 4: Send the leads to GA4

Now the leads need somewhere to go. Create a Google Analytics: GA4 Event tag with your Measurement ID, use the trigger from Step 3, and add the form details as event parameters from Data Layer Variables.

[[img:uft-ga4-tag|Only form details go to GA4. The imported tag is named generate_lead and sends form_cta, form_platform and form_position.]]
Keep contact details out of GA4. The payload can include ec_name, ec_email and ec_phone. GA4's terms prohibit personal data in event parameters, so don't add them here.

On this store the GA4 event is named form_submit, and generate_lead stays on the thank-you page. Pick one as your key event, so GA4 doesn't count the same lead twice.
Step 5: Separate the landing page from the main site

Here's where the original problem comes back. One script sees both forms, but the client still wants to know whether a lead came from the ad landing page or the main site, and usually wants separate Google Ads conversions.

So add one Custom Event trigger per surface, using that platform's event name and Page Hostname:

[[img:uft-trigger-list|Squarespace on the main site and SwipePages on the landing page, each with its own trigger. Domains anonymised.]][[img:uft-trigger-lp|Event name plus hostname, so this only fires for leads on the landing page.]]

If both surfaces use the same platform, the hostname does all the separating. If a client later moves to a different form tool, the same tag detects it, and you only update the trigger.
Step 6: Add the Google Ads conversions

With those triggers in place, each Google Ads conversion tag only needs its own label. Create a Google Ads Conversion Tracking tag for each surface, and make sure you have a Conversion Linker on all pages.

[[img:uft-gads-tag|One tag for the landing page. The website tag is the same with its own label and trigger. Label hidden.]]

Here's the full setup with everything in place:

[[img:uft-tag-list|One form listener, with GA4, Google Ads and Meta all working from its events. IDs anonymised.]]

For Meta, pass ec_event_id as the event ID. It's a unique ID on every event, which lets Meta match browser and server events.
Step 7: Map the contact data for Enhanced Conversions

This is the part most worth slowing down for. Create one Data Layer Variable for each field, then a User-Provided Data variable set to Manual configuration, and use it either in your conversion tags or in a Google Ads User-provided Data Event tag on the Step 3 trigger, which is what this store uses.

Data Layer VariableUser-Provided Data field
ec_emailEmail
ec_phonePhone
ec_first_nameFirst Name
ec_last_nameLast Name
ec_streetStreet
ec_cityCity
ec_regionRegion
ec_postal_codePostal Code
ec_countryCountry
[[img:uft-user-data|This older setup maps email and phone only. The current import file maps all nine.]]
Check each variable's key. A copied variable that still reads the wrong key won't show an error. My own first import file had Dlv - ec_phone reading ec_email, so phone numbers never reached the variable.

Emails are lowercased and checked, and phones are normalized to E.164, using a country field on the form when there is one. Password, card, SSN, IBAN and similar field names are always stripped, and you can add more with redactFields.
Step 8: Set up consent, and remove any test settings

Now for the mistake I promised. The script auto-detects Google Consent Mode v2, OneTrust and Cookiebot. With analytics consent denied, events are held and replayed if consent is later granted. With personal data consent denied, events still fire, without contact data, and carry ec_pii_redacted: true.

For any other consent tool, you can override it:

window.EC_FORM_CONSENT_CHECK = function () {
  return { analytics: true, pii: false };
};
This is the mistake that passes every test. That snippet is useful for testing, and dangerous if it stays. I found exactly this in a leftover test tag, including in my own first import file. The form still submits, *_form_success still fires and the conversion still counts, but name, email and phone are removed from every event. Enhanced Conversions has nothing to send, and nothing tells you. If your container has a tag like Consent Init, open it and read what it returns.
Step 9: Test it, including the data inside the event

This is why a passing test needs a closer look. Click Preview and connect to each surface, the main site and the landing page.

  1. Load the page. Expect ec_tracker_initialized, with your platform in ec_platforms_detected.
  2. Run this in the console to see detected platforms, attached forms, consent and the last event:
    window._ecFormTracker.status()
  3. Submit with a required field empty. Expect that platform's _form_failed event, and no success.
  4. Submit a valid, clearly labelled test lead. Expect one _form_success, once.
  5. Click that event, open Data Layer, and check that ec_email and ec_phone hold the right values and that ec_pii_redacted isn't there.
  6. Check which tags fired: the right Google Ads tag for that hostname, and your GA4 tag without contact data.

This is what a healthy lead looks like, from a labelled test on the example landing page:

[[img:uft-preview-payload|ec_name, ec_email and ec_phone all filled, with no ec_pii_redacted. Test values, on v3.1.0.]]
Don't stop at step 4. The event firing tells you the listener works. Only step 5 tells you Enhanced Conversions has anything to send.
Step 10: Publish, then check what's live

Remove any older form tags and thank-you triggers for the same forms, then submit the workspace. Submit one more test lead on the live site, with Preview closed, and confirm it shows up in GA4 Realtime and on the client's side.

From then on, segment GA4 by ec_detection_method now and then. A sudden shift usually means a platform changed its markup, which is the main way a script like this goes out of date.

What I tested, and what to know

I've tested the listener on live forms and it works, including a labelled test lead in November 2026 that fired the Google Ads, GA4 and Meta tags with contact data intact. Also, the v3 line runs in 12 of the client containers I checked in November 2026. By tag name those run v3.0.0 to v3.1.0. The download is v3.3.0, which adds Contact Form 7 and more contact fields without changing existing event names or keys, so test it on your own forms before relying on it.

Limits to plan for:

  • The GoHighLevel iframe message format is reverse-engineered. If GoHighLevel changes it, that path stops until it's updated, and iframe failures can't be seen from the parent page.
  • Inferred successes can occasionally be wrong, and cross-domain redirects can't use the stored backup.
  • Bot and spam submissions that pass the platform's own validation still count. ec_fast_submit flags very quick submits as a hint.
  • Platforms change their markup, so test after any big form change.
Frequently asked questions

Does it work on one platform only?

Yes, but a single-platform listener is roughly half the size if that's all the site will ever run.

Do I need to change my old triggers if I'm on v2?

No event names or keys changed, so v2 triggers keep working. Update the regex to pick up the newer platforms.

Should I turn on hashPii?

Only if something downstream needs SHA-256 values in the dataLayer. Google tags can hash the plain values themselves, which is why it's off by default.

Why not just use GTM's Form Submission trigger?

It often misses AJAX forms and iframes, and it doesn't know whether the platform accepted the lead.

Is it free?

Yes, MIT licensed and on GitHub.
closing: If you'd rather have this installed and checked for you, or your lead numbers still don't add up after following this guide, I can help.
